headline: Resolution Capital sees global listed infrastructure entering a structural growth phase driven by electrification, AI power demand, and energy security
reasoning: Mark Jones argues that infrastructure is no longer just a defensive yield play but is becoming a prerequisite for economic growth. He expects earnings growth to accelerate from high single digits historically to low double digits or even mid-teens over the next five to 20 years. The convergence of electrification of transport, manufacturing, heating and cooling, plus AI's power demand, digital infrastructure, water/waste, and energy security are all arriving simultaneously. Unlike general equities where capex increases create uncertainty, regulated infrastructure assets have monopoly-like characteristics with known returns in advance, locking in earnings growth. US utilities are planning to spend in the next five years what they spent in the entire previous decade, which Jones says effectively doubles earnings growth.
quote: Infrastructure is now seen as an enabler of economic growth. Whether that be power infrastructure for new industry formation or transport infrastructure for urbanisation and productivity, we're seeing opportunity globally to deploy capital for really appealing returns. 'Decade of power' or 'golden age of utilities' is also what we hear from management teams that we speak to. Most developed economies of the world need to electrify everything. We can see that in transport, we can see that in heating, cooling, and in manufacturing, and now we're seeing it in AI.
episode_title: The ‘undisruptable’ growth trade that gets better the more AI spends

headline: Data demand is driving secular growth in digital infrastructure, forming one of several simultaneous structural tailwinds for the infrastructure asset class
reasoning: Jones identifies digital infrastructure driven by data demand as one of the key structural tailwinds alongside electrification, water/waste (circular economy), and energy security. AI's insatiable appetite for power is layering on top of existing electrification demand that is yet to be fully built out. The convergence of these trends arriving simultaneously is what Jones expects to drive earnings growth acceleration from high single digits to low double digits and potentially mid-teens over the next five to 20 years.
quote: Wherever there's a need for investment in infrastructure, that's when the asset class does well. Most developed economies of the world need to electrify everything. We can see that in transport, we can see that in heating, cooling, and in manufacturing, and now we're seeing it in AI.
episode_title: The ‘undisruptable’ growth trade that gets better the more AI spends

headline: Hyperscaler capex on data centres is an unusual tailwind for US utilities — shifting cost burden away from households and reducing regulatory risk
reasoning: Jones argues that with big tech (Meta, Microsoft, Google, Amazon) footing the bill for power infrastructure rather than average households, utilities earn higher revenues while household electricity bills come down. This self-reinforcing cycle means governments have little incentive to intervene on pricing, which is the key regulatory risk for the sector. This dynamic makes the current AI-driven capex cycle unusually favourable for utility earnings growth compared to historical infrastructure build-outs where households bore the cost.
quote: Infrastructure companies have higher earnings growth, households are paying less for electricity, and importantly, governments and households are happy, and we as investors receive stronger earnings growth. When households have to pay too much for the infrastructure… governments can get involved. And when governments get involved in the pricing of infrastructure, that's when uncertainty occurs.
episode_title: The ‘undisruptable’ growth trade that gets better the more AI spends
